text: Let your AI agent read your WhatsApp messages. This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything. Ask your agent things like: Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to. It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications. Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else. You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone. git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp cd whatsapp-mcp npm install # 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc. npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV # 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters. npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD # 3. Deploy. npm run deploy Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev . Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps: Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it. Connect your agent. In Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point them at the same /mcp URL. If you want your own domain, see the comments at the bottom of wrangler.jsonc . Importing a large history decodes a lot of data in one go, and the default CPU limit on Workers is too small for it. wrangler.jsonc raises it, and raising it needs the paid plan, which is a few dollars a month. I haven't tried the free plan. If you're on it, remove the limits block and expect the first import to be fragile. This isn't official. WhatsApp has no API for reading your own personal messages. This uses the same protocol WhatsApp Web uses, through an open source library (Baileys). That's against WhatsApp's terms. For a linked device that only reads, the practical risk is low, but it isn't zero. Use it on your own account, and don't use it to send messages. You get what WhatsApp sends. The first link imports whatever history WhatsApp decides to hand a new device. It may not be everything. It only does this once per link. To import again, relink (your stored messages are kept, and a re-import fills in anything missing). Some chats show up as phone numbers. WhatsApp doesn't give a linked device every contact name, and most of these are one-off messages from people you never saved. For the ones that matter, your agent can fix it: it lists the unnamed chats, looks the numbers up in your contacts with whatever contacts tool it already has (a Google Contacts or Gmail connector, for example), and saves the names. The server never connects to a contacts service itself. See "Naming chats" below. Media isn't downloaded. Photos, voice notes and documents appear as labels like [image] or [voice note 12s] , with the caption if there was one. Nothing is transcribed. It's for one person. One deployment is one WhatsApp account and one owner. That's deliberate: each deployment holds a full message history and a live login to the account, so everyone should run their own. Relinking. If your phone says the device was removed, or you want to start over, ask your agent to run relink , or open /setup and choose "Unlink and scan again". You scan a new QR code. Stored messages are kept. Every read tool first tops up from WhatsApp if the stored copy is more than ten minutes old. WhatsApp only gives this server the names it knows. The rest show up as phone numbers. Rather than have the server log in to a contacts service (which means a cloud project, consent screens and, for Google, an app review), it hands the job to your agent, which usually already has a way to reach your contacts. Say "find names for my unnamed chats". The agent calls unnamed_chats , matches the numbers against your contacts, and saves what it finds with set_contact_names . It won't find everyone: most unnamed chats are a single message from a stranger. Agents get nudged toward this on their own. The server's instructions mention it, and so does every "no chat found" and "no matches" result, because that's the moment an agent is stuck on a name. link_status also says how many chats are unnamed. Everything below is for whoever is changing the code, including an AI agent working on a fork. The top of this file is for the person who owns the deployment. MCP client ──OAuth──> Worker (src/index.ts) ├─ /mcp ───────────> mcp.ts: tools, one fresh McpServer per request ├─ /, /setup, /authorize, /login/*, /pair/* (landing, sign-in, pairing UI) └─ cron 04:00 UTC ──> pull() │ RPC v WhatsAppStore (Durable Object, one instance named "owner") ├─ SQLite: auth keys, messages, chats, contacts, FTS5 index └─ Baileys socket, opened only during a session (pairing or pull) │ WebSocket v WhatsApp servers One Durable Object holds everything. Its SQLite is both the Baileys auth store and the message store. The Worker is stateless apart from a KV namespace the OAuth provider uses for tokens and a short-lived "pending sign-in" record. All WhatsApp traffic happens inside runSession() in whatsapp-do.ts . There are two kinds: Callers share one session: a second pull() while one is running gets the same promise. A pairing session outlives the HTTP request that started it. startPairing sets a Durable Object alarm, and alarm() awaits the session promise. An in-flight alarm handler is what keeps the object alive. The pairing page only watches; closing it doesn't stop the import. Idle detection counts only data events ( messaging-history.set , messages.upsert ), not connection chatter. Counting everything keeps a session open forever, because presence and contact updates never stop. All in the Durable Object's SQLite ( store.ts , initSchema ). Ingest is idempotent. Re-importing history upserts: it fills in a missing sender or push_name and never duplicates. That is what makes relinking safe. These all cost real time to find. Read them before touching the Baileys parts. Keep a deployment's own values (domain, KV id, email) in wrangler.local.jsonc , which is gitignored, and deploy with npm run deploy:local . wrangler.jsonc is the template other people start from. With PIN set, these return JSON and need the header x-pin: <PIN> : Local development: npm run dev with a .dev.vars containing OWNER_PASSWORD=... (12+ characters). It runs a local Durable Object with its own empty storage, so you can exercise the sign-in flow and see a real QR code, but linking a phone from local dev makes a second linked device. To test the pairing UI states without a phone, serve the page with a mocked /pair/status . Everything the page needs is that one JSON shape: paired , running , progress , qrSvg , messages , chats .
